We look before and after, And pine for what is not.

But as we get older we learn to be satisfied with something nearer than the moon. The horizon of our hopes and ambitions narrows, but the sky above is not less deep, and we make the wonderful discovery that the things that matter are very near to us. It is the homing of the spirit. We have been avid of the "topless grandeurs" of life, and we return to find that the spiritual satisfactions we sought were all the time within very easy reach. And in cultivating those satisfactions intensively we make another discovery. We find that this is the true way to the "topless grandeurs" themselves, for those topless grandeurs are not without us but within.

But I am afraid I am sermonising, and I do not want to sermonise, though if ever a man may be allowed to sermonise it is when he is completing his half-century. Let me as an antidote recall a little story which the present Bishop of Chester once told me over the dinner table, for it contains a practical recipe for keeping the heart young. He was in his earlier days associated with Archdeacon Jones of Liverpool. The Archdeacon, then over eighty, had been tutor to Gladstone, and one day the future Bishop turned the conversation into a reminiscent channel, and sought to evoke the Archdeacon's memories of the long past. Presently the Archdeacon abruptly changed the subject by asking, "What was the concert of the Philharmonic like last night?" And then, in answer to the obvious surprise which the question had aroused, he added, "Although I am an old man, I want to keep my heart young, and the best way of doing that is not to let one's thoughts live in the past, but to keep them in tune with the life around one."

The truth is that every stage of the journey has its own interests. Probably none is better than another, but my own preference has always been for that stage which I happen to be doing at the time. When I was twenty I thought there was no age like twenty, and now I am fifty I have transferred my enthusiasm to fifty. There is no age like it, I feel, for all-round enjoyment. And I have a strong conviction that if I have the good fortune to reach sixty I shall be found declaring that there is no age like sixty. And why not? It is pleasant to see the sun on the morning hills, but it is not less pleasant to walk home when the shadows are lengthening and the cool of the evening has come.

message.content:
As we reflect on our lives, we often find ourselves yearning for what is unattainable. However, with the passage of time, we gradually come to appreciate the importance of valuing what is closer at hand. The scope of our dreams and aspirations may seem to contract, yet the vastness of the sky remains unchanged. In this process, we discover that the elements that truly enrich our lives are often within our immediate reach. This realization represents a return to our inner selves. We may have once chased after the "topless grandeurs" of existence, only to recognize that the spiritual fulfillment we sought has been accessible all along. By nurturing these simple joys, we uncover a profound truth: the grandeur we yearn for lies not in distant places but within our own hearts.

I find myself veering into preachiness, which is not my intention, although reaching the milestone of fifty years can easily provoke such sentiments. To counteract this inclination, I would like to share a story told to me by the current Bishop of Chester during a dinner conversation, as it offers practical wisdom on maintaining a youthful spirit. In his younger days, he worked alongside Archdeacon Jones of Liverpool, who, despite being over eighty and once a tutor to Gladstone, exhibited remarkable vitality. During a nostalgic exchange, the Bishop attempted to draw out the Archdeacon's past experiences. However, the Archdeacon unexpectedly shifted gears by inquiring about the previous night's Philharmonic concert. When the Bishop expressed surprise at this diversion, the Archdeacon explained, "Though I am an old man, I strive to keep my heart young, and the best way to achieve that is to remain engaged with the present rather than dwell on the past."

Every phase of life has its unique attractions, and while it is difficult to declare one stage as superior to another, I have always found myself favoring the age I currently inhabit. In my twenties, I believed there was no better age than twenty; now that I am fifty, my enthusiasm has naturally shifted to this current decade. I genuinely feel that fifty is the prime age for experiencing joy in its many forms. I hold a firm belief that should I reach sixty, I will undoubtedly proclaim that there is no age quite like sixty. And why should that not be the case? While there is a certain delight in watching the sun rise over the hills in the morning, there is just as much pleasure to be found in the evening stroll home, when the shadows grow longer and the coolness of dusk settles in.
